real_estate.homebuilder: A California study of 74,070 fire claims found 71% of destroyed homes were underinsured.
real_estate.commentary:
Mortgage rates start the week where Friday left them. Mortgage News Daily has the 30-year at 7.43% and the 15-year at 7.10% as of September 25, with Monday's reading due this afternoon. The 10-Year is not helping: it was near 5.26% at 7:54 AM PT, above Thursday's 5.18% close, which was already the highest since 2007.

The newsletter's housing story is a California one. Kenneth Klein, a law professor at California Western School of Law, obtained state Department of Insurance data on 74,070 fire claims on owner-occupied homes from 2018 to 2023. Of the homes destroyed, 71.3% were underinsured, by about 19% on average.

Wildfire made it worse but did not create it: catastrophe losses came up short 78% of the time, ordinary house fires 68%. The weak link was the insurer's own rebuild estimate at the point of sale, which ran below the final loss 75% to 95% of the time. The newsletter wrote that only about 90% of homes have insurance; in the study, 90% is the share of policies that carried extended or guaranteed replacement cost.

Locally the weekend was quiet. Fremont's 257 live listings did not change between Sunday's and Monday's MLS exports, and the five city ledger stands at 717, up from 714 on Friday.

What this means for you: ask your insurer for a fresh replacement cost estimate rather than trusting the one written with the policy, and check whether extended replacement cost is on it. Buyers should line up quotes before contingencies come off; sellers who have a recent estimate can hand it to buyers as one less worry.

• Board wide: 2,762 listings across our 15 city table, counting active and in contract together, with 184 coming soon and 224 brand new.

stocks.news:
Monday opened lower, with oil and Treasury yields both climbing. By 7:54 AM PT the Nasdaq was down 1.26%, the S&P 0.95% and the Dow 0.72%.

Meta is the chart. At Thursday's close it was up 36% for September, on pace for its best month since July 2013, on enthusiasm for its Muse AI app. It fell 3.33% Friday and was down another 4.36% this morning at $718.88, trimming the month's gain to about 26%. The spending behind the AI push keeps climbing: capital spending went from $39.2 billion in 2024 to $72.2 billion in 2025, and Meta guides $130 billion to $145 billion for 2026, with $50.9 billion spent through June. For plenty of Bay Area buyers, that stock is part of the down payment.

feature_image.alt: Bar chart of Meta capital spending including finance lease payments: $28.1 billion in 2023, $39.2 billion in 2024 and $72.2 billion in 2025, up 84%. For 2026 Meta guides $130 billion to $145 billion, up 80% to 101%, of which $50.9 billion was spent from January to June.
feature_image.caption: Meta's capital spending rose 84% in 2025 to $72.2 billion, and its 2026 guidance is $130 billion to $145 billion, with $50.9 billion spent through June. Meta has not guided past 2026.
feature_image.source: Source: Meta Platforms Form 10-K for 2025 and earnings releases of January 28, April 29 and July 29, 2026.

economy.commentary:
Monday is reversing Friday. Brent's November contract was up 2.63% at $107.06, taking back Friday's 2.14% drop, and gold was down 3.81% at $4,156.70 as yields climbed. The newsletter stamped its gold and 10-Year prints 4:00 PM Eastern on Sunday, when neither market trades; they were overnight quotes.

Fun is getting pricier, and people are paying anyway. Sales at sporting goods, hobby, music and book stores rose 10.7% in the year to August, against 6.0% for all retail, per the Census Bureau, and Bank of America says hobby spending on its cards rose 7.9%. Airline fares are up 23.4%, not the 26.5% making the rounds, which was June's reading.

Closer to home, recreation prices in the San Francisco, Oakland and Hayward area rose 7.5% over the year to August, more than twice the area's 3.4% overall inflation and nearly three times the national 2.7%. Funflation, it turns out, has a Bay Area premium.

feature_image.alt: Horizontal bar chart of changes from a year earlier, August 2026. Prices: airline fares up 23.4%, recreation in the Bay Area up 7.5%, all items up 3.4%, recreation nationally up 2.7%. Spending: sporting goods, hobby, music and book stores up 10.7%, hobby spending on Bank of America cards up 7.9%, all retail and restaurant sales up 6.0%.
feature_image.caption: Hobby stores and hobby card spending are growing faster than retail overall, and Bay Area recreation prices rose 7.5%, nearly three times the national rate. Airfares are August's 23.4%.
feature_image.source: Sources: BLS Consumer Price Index; Census Bureau advance retail sales, September 16, 2026; Bank of America card data as reported by CNBC.
